utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Stoparic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I remind you that the solemn undertaking which you took yesterday continues to apply to your evidence today and for the rest of your evidence. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Lukic, to continue your cross-examination --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a question for the Bench and an appeal at the same time. It would take but a few moments and I would kindly ask to go into private session, if we could. Since you've advised me specifically that I wasn't to discuss my testimony with anyone and I tried to come up with an answer that I was looking for from myself. Therefore, perhaps I could clarify that in private session briefly. Now, I wanted to present the problem that I have, and I promise to be brief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Why is it necessary to go into private session?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I believe is the problem is what I need to understand -- what I need to explain for you to understand. If I speak about the issue now in open session, then there would be no point in going into private session. And again, I can promise that I will be brief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, since you're anxious that you may say something inappropriate in the course of this discussion, we will go into private session for it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I will try my best not -- to follow your guidances given to us today and hopefully I won't make any mistakes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Stoparic.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We meet again it seems. Briefly I would like to go back to a topic we discussed yesterday. I don't believe there is anything in dispute concerning that, but I wanted to elaborate one thing we discussed yesterday. You mentioned the tragic events in Podujevo yesterday, and you stated that your superiors probably helped to prevent any further massacres and tragedies by removing the Skorpions from the area.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that only God knows what could have happened had they not done so.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Therefore, I think we may conclude that in any case your superiors, that is those from the SAJ, never ordered that civilians could be fired upon?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is absolutely true.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Therefore, we may conclude that the killings of those people was not intentional or planned by the SAJ or the police for that matter?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've been testifying several times concerning that event, and I kept repeating that no one had ordered anything of that nature. I never ordered such a thing, and no one did. I'm quite positive about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If I go back to the numbers from the sketch you made, could you be able -- would you be able to follow me as to who I'm referring to?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you were to use the names, I could follow, but as to the numbers, I'm not sure. If I had them in front of me together with the names, then that might work.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we could provide the witness a copy of both the redacted and the unredacted versions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, what's necessary is an unredacted one so that he can relate the number to the name, and the examiner can use the number.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's right. We have the number on the unredacted version. So if we could have the usher hand him that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, please. Just for the avoidance of doubt, does the unredacted one have a separate exhibit number?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, I don't believe it does, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Then certainly the statement I have has a redacted copy only attached to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The unredacted version has a separate ERN number, but I don't know if that's been loaded into e-court. Perhaps we can mark it later and file it under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I should indicate I believe Defence counsel's put in the statement to which the original unredacted version was an attachment as well. So that should be in e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's the -- you mean the statement of the 6th of July?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, not the statement of the 6th of July, but his --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But his 2003 --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: 2004 statement I believe, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, we haven't reached that one yet. The one we were exploring yesterday was 6D7, which is the November 2003.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, I was just indicating for the convenience of counsel if he wanted to look at an unredacted version to match it up with the numbers to make it easier for him to do the questioning. It's the attachment to the statement of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: 24th of February, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It looks like it was several days in February and a day in May in 2004.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Now, Mr. Lukic, do you have a number -- well, do you have a statement with the unredacted drawing or sketch attached to it?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I was just informed that we only have the statement without the chart.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Let's proceed then on the basis of the document that's just been handed to the witness, and the Prosecution can have that loaded into e-court under seal and give it a number there, and that can be intimated to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And if it's helpful to Mr. Lukic, I can give him an unredacted copy right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I suspect he might need it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I do have one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Oh, you do have that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, please carry on, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Does the Court need one, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That would be helpful, yes. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. One more thing before we proceed with this witness. On page 6, line 6 -- 5 and 6 actually of the transcript it says: "I never ordered such a thing." But I didn't ask the witness whether he ordered and he didn't answer in that manner. He said: "I never heard that anybody ordered." I would like just that correction to be made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry, line -- you're on page 5 --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No, page 6, line 5 and 6.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, that's consistent with my note of the evidence, I have to say, what's in the transcript. I don't really see that there's any material difference. He said he didn't order such a thing and no one did. It's pretty definite. The note I've made is: No one ordered the Podujevo massacre, so it's consistent with my recollection of the evidence. So let's carry on as it is, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stoparic, I will now mention a number from the sketch. According to what you can remember, the murders at Podujevo were committed by the number 1. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One could say so, yes, although I don't believe the main person led the whole thing is marked under the number 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it correct that members of the Serbian MUP, of the Serbian police, immediately after the incident took all necessary measures to provide assistance and medical assistance to the civilians injured by the person and other people under the number 1?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was an active SAJ officer who's a physician in civilian life - I believe his name was Dragan - and he tried to save those that were still alive.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: According to the judgement tendered yesterday by the OTP, which is P291 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: P951, this incident -- in that incident, five children survived and were administered first aid subsequently?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I participated in that trial in Belgrade, I've learned that there were several children there. At first I thought that only one or two had survived, and you know very well that we were driven away by Tutinac himself and we didn't have the time to see everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You've already stated that the SAJ commander was upset, that he cursed at the people from the unit for the events at Podujevo. Were you under the impression that he was upset because of the fact that civilians were killed?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I still remember clearly his words, and I can quote them quite precisely if you want me to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I don't believe that is necessary, but you may as well if you want the Chamber to hear that.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: His behaviour was such that one could conclude that he was very worried about the things that took place, and in his brief speech he told us: You are not the people to be counted on, or: One can't work with you. I was under the impression that he wasn't very happy about the things that took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were you under the impression that this incident was a shock for the other policemen as well?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a person, a man, whose nickname was Vuk, Wolf. He was a very good professional, an SAJ officer, and he was even -- he used even harsher words. He even took one of the children out in the street to bring him to the ambulance that was there. None of the members of the SAJ, as far as I could see, was happy about that -- well, not happy, but they were probably horrified. People at that time couldn't have known who from the Skorpions did that. And when our officers spoke to us, they addressed the entire unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Therefore, we may conclude that the people who didn't participate in the killing were all angry and upset over what had happened?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've replied already as regards the SAJ unit. As for the Skorpions, those who didn't participate were not happy about it, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The withdrawal of your unit from Podujevo back to Serbia, did you see that as a sort of punishment, a sanction?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At first, when we arrived at Prolom Banja, we stayed there for another few days. And my opinion was that someone at the higher levels was probably contemplating what to do with us and what would take place. I expected sanctions, an investigation, and prison sentences for the perpetrators. And already in Prolom Banja we knew who the perpetrators were. Some of them even boasted about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The person under the number 1 --

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can mention his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The person under the number 1 was arrested by the Serbian police because of his role in all these events.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You probably mean the person under the number 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You can see in the transcript the number 4, but what I think you wanted to say --

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Both people under the number 1 and 4 were arrested and spent some time in custody in Belgrade. And after they were released, I spoke to them in Novi Sad.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you at that time go to Belgrade perhaps?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, during the war.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the war?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers please be asked to pause between question and answer and not to overlap. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Be cautious about overlapping when the interpreters have to deal with both question and answer in the one language. Thank you. Try just to pause, please, Mr. Stoparic, before you answer the question so that the interpretation can be completed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The person under the number 1 on the drawing, he was also sentenced because of the events that took place at Podujevo. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: As regards that testimony, you were provided police protection by the Serbian police. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Therefore, we may conclude that the Serbian police at the time you testified never exerted any pressure upon you not to testify about the incident?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: None of the statements I've given concerning this mentions any of -- anything of that sort. I've already stated who tried to pressure me.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I just wanted to have that clarified. Some of the questions may see superfluous, but -- to you it may seem unnecessary, although we still need to clarify that here. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may have a moment, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: To go back to your report, yesterday we stopped at paragraph 76 of your report of the 21st of November, 1993 [as interpreted], that is Exhibit 6D7.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's being translated as "report" but it should be "statement."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 76 is on the fourth page of the English text and it is also on the fourth page of the B/C/S text. Yesterday this was also referred to on the 48th page, line 4 of the transcript. In that paragraph you say: "The order was issued from the top, that 60 per cent of our personnel should be from Republika Srpska and the Republic of Serbian Krajina and 40 per cent of them from the Republic of Serbia. That is because of the fact that the people on the top in Serbia could always deny the connection because them and the Skorpions."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd like to point to a correction I think needs to be made in the transcript. It refers to the statement as being in November 1993, I'm looking at line 11 on page 13. I think the statement is in 2003. And paragraph 76 is on the 15th page of the English, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah. Thank you, Mr. Hannis. Carry on, Mr. Lukic, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Correct, it is the 15th page of the English text and page 19 and 21 of the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction, 19 and 20 of the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Stoparic, I should only like to ask you whether you ever saw an order containing anything of the sort and what is the source of your knowledge about this?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that I replied to that question yesterday. The source is Srdjan Manojlovic. But I'm quite sure that it is exactly the way I said it, verbatim. Because I wanted to bring two or three people to join -- two or three men to join the Skorpions, but of course I couldn't do that without the knowledge of the commander or of Srdjan Manojlovic or of his deputy. This is what he replied. He said in his response to my question: Why not? He said: Well, they could always claim that this is so or that this is not so, so that when I was giving my statement I believe that I gave that same explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 78 of the same statement, page 15 of the English version and the 20th page of the B/C/S version you say, the third sentence: "The Skorpions issued a military service booklet to me with my photograph and my rank. It was written in it that I was a member of the state security of the MUP of Serbia. In this military service booklet, it did not say RSK. What was written in it was the Republic of Serbia." Don't you think that it is contradictory, in fact, that somebody wanted to hide the fact that the Skorpions were a part of the Serbian forces, whereas issuing a military service booklet confirming exactly that [as interpreted]?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, don't you think an egoist could have issued a document of precisely this type?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm not authorised to respond to questions. I'm not on the stand.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me tell you. What I tried to explain to you is that many Skorpions had this service booklet in red hide with their photographs, bound in red hide, with their photographs, their ranks, and authorising them to use the communication devices of others, the transportation means of others. I presume that many of them returned those service booklets, but -- what was it I was going to say, explain. You pointed to -- you alluded to a contradiction --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it not contradictory that a state wishing to hide its connection with your unit, as Srdjan Manojlovic puts it and says, is at the same time issuing you with booklets, showing that you are indeed a part of its forces. That is contradictory to me. What do you think?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It appears to be contradictory to me as well. There were many mistakes, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But precisely because you did have such a booklet, such a document, don't you perhaps think that Srdjan Manojlovic was not telling the telling the truth?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Srdjan Manojlovic, I would not like to really debate him or his character, talk about him at any length.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Paragraph 81 of the statement, which in the B/C/S version is on page 21 --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I think that we have to intervene again regarding this transcript. It's page 15, line 25, one part of the witness's answer is missing, because at the end he said: "Everything is possible."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, thank you, Mr. Lukic. It's confirmed that that was omitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: May I proceed, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stoparic, sorry. Sometimes in this court we have to deal with matters which take our time. Then we will have probably such situations also in the future, so I apologise in advance to you for having to also bear with that. So let us go back to page -- paragraph 81 of your statement of the 21st of November, 2003, the 21st page of the B/C/S version; 15 and 16 are the English version pages. In this paragraph you say: "The order for operations -- orders for operations were received directly from Mrgud, the minister of defence of the Republic of the Serbian Krajina." Can we mention the name of this gentleman?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So this is Milan Milanovic. Was he a member of the Skorpions?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If he was a minister, why would a minister belong to the SAJ?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So he did not?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And he was not a member of the MUP either, right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said -- the minister of defence is what I said. I'm not quite sure that he was a minister of defence. He may have gone through a number of ministries in his political career.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But being a politician, he did not belong to the military either?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if he was the minister of defence, then he had the position of a commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: A minister and a politician?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but a minister of defence is a very important factor in the military, if he was indeed the minister of defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If this gentleman, Milan Milanovic, were to claim that he could have in no way whatsoever influenced the actions of these Skorpions, would he have been telling the truth?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably not.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Because in his -- in his statement given to the OTP from the 29th of June, 2005, in paragraph 11, he says, he claims, that the command was of -- by Slobodan Medic and that he reported to General Loncar. Is this true?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The names are familiar. But in order to disprove what Mr. Mrgud is saying, in every field, in every terrain, including that to Kosovo, after many years he took us there personally. Now, whether this only involved a relationship of friendship with the commander or something else, this is something for him to explain.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So you say that this gentleman did not have -- did have operative control over you?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Of course he claims something else in paragraph 12 in his statement of the 29th of June, 2005.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't blame him. He is afraid of being accused of it, of an indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now I am going to move on to paragraph 108 of the same statement, English 19, page 19, B/C/S page 26. You say there: "The so-called blockade of the transfer of military equipment to the Republika Srpska was such only in the beginning, but practically it was only for the international community but in practice thousands of lorries crossed the border over to Republika Srpska at night." So I ask you: Is the natural boundary between Serbia and the Republika Srpska the River Drina?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, and when I'm talking about the natural boundary in this particular example, I'm talking about the River Sava.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter could not hear the counsel because of the overlap.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How many bridges are there on the Sava between Serbia and the Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Between Serbia and the Republika Srpska I know about the bridge at Raca.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And there was also the Pavloviceva Cuprija, the Pavlovica bridge?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the Pavloviceva bridge on the Sava River also.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And in the municipality of Bijeljina is it there?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so. I think it's in Zvornik municipality or somewhere around there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, it doesn't matter right now. What I want to know is: Is it possible that during night thousands of lorries should cross over to the other side, across just a couple of bridges?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No one was referring to just one night. Neither did I.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Sorry, that is what I understood you to have said.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says at night, at night, during different -- on different nights, thousands of lorries crossed over.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I accept this correction. I just took it to mean one night. It is my mistake.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I myself crossed that boundary, that border, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The English translation "at night" means that it is singular, but okay. Were these --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, don't rely on me understanding it in that sense, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I stand corrected, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stoparic, were these bridges overseen at night by international monitors, observers?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we are talking about bridges, let us please return to the Raca bridge because I know much more about it than about Pavloviceva Most. Because in my life I perhaps just crossed over this Pavloviceva bridge once privately. This bridge in Raca, it would be best if I actually described to you how I myself crossed it in military uniform, with military equipment, so that everybody would be clear on how this went on and how it was seen by the European monitors.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were there any European monitors there?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You probably know where this bridge is and you know that it is behind a curve. There is a restaurant before it, some 500 metres ahead of it. There are bungalows of the customs administration, of the police, of the Serbian forces are also there. In fact, that -- they are unable to see the bridge in its entirety but just parts of it if they are standing on the road. So the European monitors also were together, there together with the MUP people and people who are manning the crossing and who worked there as a matter of routine. So it is very easy. And when one went clandestinely to the bridge, one went through the village of Visjnicevo by a forest-path and reached the other part of the bridge. One would come in front of the bridge, turn off the lights, and cross slowly and clandestinely over to the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But if you don't see the -- if you don't cross the half of the bridge which they also can see, what good does it do you?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they never saw us. And if they did see something, they were given some explanations, I'm quite sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So you are saying today that the monitors were not doing their job properly, right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say that. I cannot claim that that the European monitors didn't do their jobs properly. But that they were misled, I can claim that, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt, Your Honour, but maybe I'm burning counsel's bridges before he's crossed them, but I fail to see the relevance of this at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The difficulty I think is that you did lead evidence about this period of time, and this seems to be a challenge to credibility and reliability that's based on exploring what's been said in statements and trying to expose these as in some way unreliable. So while you may have a certain view about how effective it is, I doubt if it can be said to be irrelevant, if that's the basis. Now, please carry on, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: And can the interpreter please ask counsel to slow down and not to overlap with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 109 of the same statement, English text 19, 20, B/C/S 26 and 27, you referred to your contacts and your travel to Tara and your encounter with a worker of the State Security Service. However, later on you say after this talk with him - let us shorten it - you became a reserve member of the JSO, the special operations unit of the State Security Service?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I called it a reservist.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In the next paragraph, 110, in page 20 of the English version, 27 of the B/C/S version, you said that you left the JSO after the signature of the Erdut agreement but that you sign an agreement for you to be a reservist of the JSO. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the signing of the Erdut agreement, I was taken - and not only I, many of us were taken - to a base called Bajdos. This is a winery near Ilok, a wine cellar near Ilok. And there I saw a man and there we gave back the equipment that we were issued with. He gave us certificates to the effect that we were members of the JSO from so-and-so to such-and-such a date, and he told us if need be they had a lists of our names and that they would call us again.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But I'm not quite clear about this. How did you -- how were you translated [as interpreted] from the JSO to the reserve force of the JSO, the reserve unit?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is nothing unclear about it. Once a reservist, you'll be a reservist again.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 110, the last sentence reads -- that was at the time when you were a JSO reservist. "I've also signed up for the JSO reserve so that they could draft me if they needed me in case of war." Since you were a JSO reservist, why did you need to sign a separate agreement for you to become a JSO reservist?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Agreement, contract, well, this sentence is a bit unclear to me as well, but it is nevertheless true. I was supposed to have been a JSO reservist. As regards the need in case of war, that's what I was told by that civilian man who issued us with the certificates and who took the equipment. The way I put it here is the way I remember it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you sign that contract?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The contract that I'd be a reservist?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what it was that I signed. Maybe it was just a certificate or a receipt, but I think this was as I put it here, although it doesn't have to be true. It was a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If something was a long time ago, then you can say "I don't remember," but you explicitly state here that you moved from the reserve forces to the reserve forces [as interpreted] by signing a contract. I was just try to clarify that.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know very well what the explanation was, and you know why things may sound a bit odd in a statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If you have no further clarifications, I would like to move on.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: By all means.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 111 of the statement you state that three buses left Sid. I will also refer to other paragraphs.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Should the Chamber deem it necessary to it, we can a wait for it to be put on the screen, but this can be easily checked later in order to save time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 18 in the statement of the 20th of February, 2004, which in this case is Exhibit 6D5, you state that two buses left Sid; whereas in paragraph 39 of the statement of the 6th of July, 2006, which is the compiled statement on page 7 of the English and the B/C/S you state that there were three buses but that the third one was not full. Which of the two is correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This refers to our first departure to Kosovo and Prolom Banja. What I do know is that one bus was sent away. The commander told the driver to go away. It wasn't -- the bus wasn't full, there were simply not enough men. Maybe I said two and then on another occasion I said three. In any case, those buses were there but not all of them arrived in Prolom Banja. Believe me, sometimes it's difficult to provide a statement. You get confused, although I know it for certain that one bus was sent away because there were not enough people who responded to the draft call. If there were 120 men, you can do your own math to see how many buses are needed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Therefore, how many buses were there?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my opinion, three of them left, although I am quite certain that one was sent away. I can't remember at this time how it went exactly the first time we went down to Kosovo. We stopped at Sid by the commander's house and there was another bus there as well. So anything is possible, but I can't remember. I don't pay much attention to such detail. Maybe someone asked me about how many buses, gave this or that answer, it didn't mean much to me. Perhaps it does to you, but I can't be any more precise.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. This is precisely my job here. In the next paragraph of the same statement, in the English page 20, in the B/C/S page 27, you state: "In a field outside Belgrade we put on uniforms and were given weapons." In paragraph 22 of the statement of the 22nd of -- of the 20th of February, 2004, in the English that is page 4, in the B/C/S page 5, you state: "We went as far as Prolom Banja dressed in civilian clothes."

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand your question. Some of us put uniforms on. When I said we put uniforms on, that means we were given, we were issued with uniforms, and we were outside in a field. And I believe this was the safest place because there were NATO air-raids at that time. Some of the people put the uniform on, although we were told to travel to Prolom Banja dressed in civilian clothes. And probably at that time I didn't know what the exact destination was. Why in one statement it says we put it on and in the other one it says we were dressed as civilians, well, both is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What about the weapons. Did you receive weapons or not?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Were we issued weapons? Well, we each took our own weapon. Is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think there was a blue truck that followed us, and then we were issued with weapons at Prolom Banja.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But in this paragraph you say that you were issued with weapons there and then?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is what I said?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is possible. As a soldier, if I say I was issued with a weapon, it doesn't have to mean that I took it physically, personally. It was there. It was supposed to be my weapon, and that is as best as I can explain. In any case, the weapons travelled with us. It would have also been strange to travel in such conditions, having in mind the activities of NATO and the KLA. To travel without weapons would have been silly. I'm quite certain now that as we were leaving for Kosovo there was a blue truck at the rear with our weapons in the same convoy. Of course we kept our distance because of the NATO bombings.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Being issued with a weapon, doesn't that presuppose that the number of that weapon be linked up with the name of the person that was issued with it?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From my experience, that seldom happened. You were simply given a rifle. There is no number, there is no paper stating this or that person was issued with this or that weapon. At that moment, the distribution of weapons was carried out by Srdjan Manojlovic. I don't remember him making any list of numbers, although he was supposed to.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Earlier you mentioned that at a certain point you gave that weapon back. If you were not issued officially with a weapon, how could you give it back?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I was given a weapon, I will always return it to the person who issued me with that weapon or to the commander. Whether someone put my name next to any number of a rifle, I don't know, but I gave the weapon back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Excuse me, I just have a question. Did these rifles have not even their own numbers? Did these weapons have their own numbers? Because every weapon has a number as it is manufactured. They had no numbers at all, you think?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, of course they had numbers. But the person distributing the weapons, who was at that time some sort of a headquarters master, wasn't making that list as to which piece was issued to whom. For example, he knew that he had 150 rifles and that he was supposed to be given those 150 rifles back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Do you remember the make of these weapons, make of these rifles, where were they made, what name, what quality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Those were automatic rifles of domestic production, M-67, 7.62 millimetres --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction, a quarter-master instead of headquarters master.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Medic --

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My name is not Medic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Stoparic. I'd like to conclude my cross-examination concerning your statement from 2003.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please be shown another statement dated the 20th of February, 2004, number 6D5. We have a copy of this statement in B/C/S for Mr. Stoparic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, does this statement deal with Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Basically this statement is regarding Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In a major part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Stoparic, I go to paragraph 21, page 4 and page 5 in the B/C/S, on page 4 in the English version.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know where that is, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were you given your statement given on the 20th of February, 2004, and then the 21st, the 24th, and the 1st of March?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I have is the 21st, 23rd, and 24th of November, 2003, and it's in English. Maybe they come together.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No, they don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Carry on, please, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, if it may assist the Court, I have a copy, hard copy, of this statement if it's easier for Mr. Stoparic to follow. Or if the usher can put it on his screen. Whatever is better for the Chambers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, he should be able to follow, I think, what's on the -- Are you having difficulty following the screen, Mr. Stoparic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I see that on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, he can see that on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 21 of your statement dated the 20th of February, 2004, you state: "We were also issued with black woolen caps with holes for the eyes, the so-called Balaclavas." This is the second sentence of the paragraph. Do you know whether any other unit in Kosovo was given such caps, apart from your unit?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not everyone in my unit had that, only the reconnaissance platoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Except for your reconnaissance platoon, do you know whether anyone else in Kosovo used such caps?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What about other Serb forces?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is possible. It wouldn't strike me as strange. They can use that because of harsh weather or -- what we call it in Serbian is the phantom cap. I don't know why it's so called. Maybe you can intimidate someone by wearing it, but it's also an ordinary cap.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: After the 24th of March, the weather is not such that would require the use of such a cap. It's already spring and temperatures are relatively high?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Did you ever go to Kosovo at that time? I was there on the 2nd of May and I saw snow.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 24. In that paragraph you state that: "50 per cent of the volunteers had no previous combat experience." Does that mean that this is not really the same unit that was in Bosnia or in Slavonia?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Definitely the composition of the unit was not the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Therefore, there were other people in that unit. Since 50 per cent of them had no combat experience, those people could not have been in Slavonia or in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most of the officers, that is commanders of attachments and platoons, did; but as regards other soldiers, most of them didn't have any experience. Most of them probably never fought in the field in any theatre.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let us go to paragraph 46 for a minute, please, that is page number 9 of the B/C/S text and the seventh page of the English version. In this paragraph you say that when you captured a village you would usually withdraw from it to a distance of about 500 metres. Why did you do that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Me?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your unit.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Me? I, as the reconnaissance platoon, those who came first, this is the normal practice of all units, those who come there first and then pull out. That is the normal routine.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Paragraph 51 of the same statement you refer to the time after you were wounded and transferred to hospital in Pristina. In the last sentence you said: "The nurse who was of Serbian ethnicity told me that I had nothing to worry about, in view of the fact that all the Albanian staff had already gone or had been expelled." Were you worried about there being any Albanian staff on the premises?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This emanates from -- stems from my question posed to her. I was worried.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Why were you worried?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because it was war. I was wounded in war. I was wounded by Albanian terrorists, and probably I had heard somewhere that the staff of hospitals, the nurses, the doctors, they had taken an oath to the effect that -- of course they had taken their medical professional oath, but of course being in war you can expect that they were perhaps not so happy with treating members of another ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did the fact that the Albanian doctors and nurses not been working -- is it not a fact that there were no Albanian staff in Serbian -- in hospitals there?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know at the time that it was a fact. We know that they actually boycotted many state institutions.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you know for a fact that they had been sent away, expelled, or did you know that they had left of their own volition?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that is a political question. I cannot give you an answer for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Paragraph 52 of this statement, which is at the same time paragraph 74 of the statement of the 6th of July, 2006. You say that a member of the PJP told you that they threw Albanians into a well and hand-grenades after them into the well also, but you cannot remember the name of the village. Can you tell us - if need be, we can go into private session - the name of the PJP member who told you this?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is paragraph 52?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Had I known his name, it would have been in that paragraph. He was my roommate for just a couple of hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 57 on the next page of the B/C/S text, page 9 of the English text, you say: "Counting the 24th of March, 1999 and the 2nd of May, 1999, I spent a total of 15 or 16 days participating in operations in Kosovo as a member of the reserve forces of the SAJ." So you were a member of the reserve forces of the SAJ and you had documentation to that effect, right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm proud of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I don't say that you should not be proud of it. What I am saying is that you were not a loose cannon, you were not a free-lancer, your unit was not some sort of a unit that just went there because you wanted to and could, but you were actually enrolled, registered, and dispatched as a reserve force of the SAJ forces, S-A-J forces?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I answer in this way; it's very brief. When I set out for Kosovo and when I found out that I would be an SAJ reservist, I said to myself: Thank God. I'm going to be a part of a very normal unit where work will be done normally and the way it should be. Of course I was paid for it and I was paid for a year thereafter. I went to the 13th of May base many times to say get my salary. I've told you about that. I was a SAJ reservist with regular documents about my status.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us move on to paragraph 59 of your statement of the 24th of February, 2004, which is identical to paragraph 71 [as interpreted] of the statement of the 6th of July, 2006, when you say that the cafe owner told you that the bodies were being transported to Obilic to be burned there. So can you tell me, please, what the name of this cafe was in which you were sitting and of the name, the cafe owner who told you this?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would gladly tell you that. It was a cafe, and it was a -- one that was working at all, it being war and all, and the barracks barely a kilometre away from there being shelled. I cannot recall its -- the owner's name. I know that he had a waitress and she had a Bosnian dialect; that's the only thing I remember. I only went there for a couple of times. I did not stay long in the base in Kosovo Polje. I went out in the field. But it is true that he said this the way I put it there. Also I can say in advance that I don't know, nor did I have any instructions, orders, to the effect that I should move anyone or bury anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It was the waitress who told you that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. It was the man who I assume was the cafe's owner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just to correct the transcript, it's actually paragraph 81 of the statement of the 6th of July.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I can help you further, I just had a rush of memory, as it were, if you agree, a surge of memory. I think -- I'm not quite sure, but I think the name of that place bears an association with the nine Jugovic brothers.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The name of the cafe, you mean?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, but I'm not quite sure. I'm not absolutely sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 62 [as interpreted], which is on the following page of this text, 9 -- page number 9 of the English text. There you explicitly state, speaking about your testimony probably before the court in Prokuplje. You say: This is what I said. Giving testimony I claim that I did not remember. That is the way I responded to all questions. Can we then take it that at that time before the court in Prokuplje you were not telling the truth?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, at that trial no one discovered that I was not telling the truth. I myself came out, came forward, and said: I am not telling the truth, I was not telling the truth. I was obstructed and I was very, very scared.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 63, the following paragraph, you explain how the situation further developed after your testimony and you said: "I got in touch with some people informing them what is the truth about this incident and what the facts were." Can you tell us today who it was that you got in touch with?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can, of course I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I called the Humanitarian Law Centre and I told them: I should like to tell the truth, but what after that?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Why didn't you address the police, go to the police, the judiciary, those who were in charge of your procedure, proceedings, the man was in detention?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, exactly. That is exactly what they told me in the Humanitarian Law Centre. That they had organised some action, that they had called the state prosecutor, and in the end it turned out that I did get -- did get police protection, although there was no legal basis for that because it was the district court that was handling the case and not the special court where you could be afforded such police protection if you were a witness collaborator or whatever it is that they call them.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Then you gave a statement to the Humanitarian Law Centre, right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, probably, about this case. If they asked me, I don't remember any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you tell them the truth?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection and as I'm saying it here and the way I put it -- I say it -- I said it before the court in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We should go back to that statement a bit later. Now in paragraph 65 of this statement, page 10 of the English text, page 12 of the B/C/S version, there you say that -- you refer to 100.000 German marks, let me not say now why you referred to that because we do not want to implicate or associate this with any people that we marked with numbers so far. At that time German marks were no longer in circulation.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew that you would be asking that. I wonder myself. Perhaps I did say so because it -- money in our minds was always equal to marks. Perhaps it was euros. I'm not sure. Probably euro was already in circulation at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So you're not quite sure that the amount offered was 100.000 marks?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was 100.000. Whether it was German marks, probably it was a slip of the tongue or of the pen. It was probably euros.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we have time, can we please put a new statement, this compiled statement, and only one paragraph from this statement because it is the only one which I could not find in the previous statements, and that would be exhibit of the Prosecutor 52224.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction, perhaps it is P2224.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Paragraph 22. Page 5 of the English text.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Stoparic, do you see this paragraph on your screen?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not yet. I see something now. What number is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Page -- sorry, number 22.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You say: "Whenever Boca went for meetings to Belgrade, Mrgud would accompany him." Did you ever go to these meetings?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. But I would be at the base when they would go.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How do you know whom they reported to?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whenever the commander returned, he would always call a meeting of all the platoon commanders and he would inform us. He liked to sort of orate, you know. And about Frenki and Stanisic, which is written in this sentence, those are his words. He always said that they were the people in charge, that they were gods, and that one did what they said was to be done. That was as far as he was concerned. That was not how I felt about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But you did not have direct knowledge because you did not attend those meetings whether they indeed did that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I do not have any direct knowledge of that kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I think everyone here must realise that you have to exercise a measure of judgement about the extent to which you cross-examine the detail of statements that don't have a lot of direct relevance to the case that we are considering but do have some relevance, obviously, as I've already explained for points that you want to make. And we have indicated that we do wish to avoid, if possible, imposing time-limits. But I'm getting the impression you have a long way to go, and I must express my concern about the way in which the -- and the extent of detail that you've been exploring in matters not directly relevant to Kosovo. Anyway, we shall break now and we shall resume at five past -- well, it may be slightly after five but we'll resume in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And I'm sorry that we received this warning from your side because you will see that this cross-examination will be terminated very briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Stoparic, I have my last question on this topic regarding the information you received from the cafe owner. He told you that corpses were being transported in the lorries to Obilicevo to be burned. Did you know that after such information given to the UN, that there was an inspection of Obilicevo and the UN experts found nothing. It was established that no bodies were burned there. Did you know that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that from the media, yes. But, sir, you also know that these were not my words.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You're absolutely right. Thank you. This concludes my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think that after me only my colleague, Aleksic, will have a few questions, and Mr. Visnjic will have also a few questions, brief questions, for this witness. And that would conclude this cross-examination. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Mr. Aleksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Stoparic.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: My name is Aleksander Aleksic, attorney-at-law from Belgrade. I appear here on behalf of Mr. Nebojsa Pavkovic. I have a few questions for you, and I'll try to be as concise and as specific as possible in my questions, and please do the same thing in your answers. If possible, answer with a yes or no. We will use your statement, the latest statement, given according to Rule 89(F), which is P2224. My questions will concern two topics as well as several paragraphs of the statement. Before doing that, I would like you to clarify one thing for me. Today, for the transcript, you stated during the cross-examination by Mr. Lukic when he was asking you about the crossing of the bridge at Raca you stated: I was a soldier in a military uniform. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A soldier in a military uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Yes. Could you please expand on that.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see where you're going. No, I was a member of the Skorpions. There is no similarity in the uniforms. You know very well when I said "a soldier in a military uniform." At wartime we are all soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you have your statement before you given according to Rule 89(F) in the B/C/S language? I will refer to pages 12 and 13 of the B/C/S and -- if I may have a moment. And those are 11 and 12 in the English. First of all, paragraph 67, the last sentence.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I may be given a moment to find that. 67, you said?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Yes. That is the last sentence at the top of the page. Did you find that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm looking at that sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Here it says: "We encountered resistance from the UCK and had gun battles but they were not a well-trained army or force and we were superior to them in both numbers and weaponry." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: On page 13 of the B/C/S in paragraph 72 you state that you were wounded. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: By whom?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: An Albanian terrorist.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Was that a serious injury?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm permanently disabled.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Were you treated for it for the next 12 months?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, for a long time.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't hear the counsel's question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Were you forced -- or rather, you were -- you were declared unfit for the military service?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Now to move on to another topic. In paragraph 70 on the same page, number 12, you state: "We did not carry out any joint operations with the VJ."

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: In the same paragraph you state: "The Yugoslav army couldn't [realtime transcript read in error "could"] move around freely during the day in their tanks and motor vehicles."

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Because of NATO and their activities in the air-space?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Aleksic. Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Stoparic. My name is Tomislav Visnjic. I appear here for General Ojdanic.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: I have a few questions concerning the time material for the indictment regarding your movements in the given period.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic, before you go any further, I see in the transcript that the last question that Mr. Aleksic asked quotes the paragraph 70 as saying: "The Yugoslav army could move around freely during the day," whereas the version I have says "could not." Anyway, as long as that's noted. I take it that that's what you assumed was the position, Mr. Aleksic? Yeah. Thank you. Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stoparic, my questions will mainly regard your statement given to the OTP on the 6th of July, 2006. I will start with the 24th of March, 1999. As far as I understood, on that day you were in Sid. Am I correct? To assist you, that is paragraph 38, if you want to follow in your statement.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 24th of March, 1999, I suppose I was in Sid.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: On the 25th of March you had a meeting, after which you boarded the buses and went to Boca's house in Novi Sad. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, as regards the events, but I'm not absolutely certain as to the date. I have very poor memory as regards dates. But the sequence of events indeed went the way you put it, and it was close to that date.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: On that same day you were taken to a meadow south of Belgrade, where you spent some time. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was already dark, it was night-time.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Around 5.00 a.m., and that should be the 26th of March if that was during the night, you arrived at the hotel in Prolom Banja?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, very early.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: You stayed in Prolom Banja for two days. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two to three days.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: On the 28th of March you were in Podujevo where the tragic incident took place?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in Podujevo when that took place. I don't know whether that was on the 28th of March.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: In your statement in paragraph 45 you state that on the 26th of March you arrived at Podujevo [as interpreted], you stayed for two days, and after having left Prolom Banja you were taken to Kosovo and Podujevo, which would be in paragraph 46. Could you please look at paragraph 46 of the statement.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have that statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would kindly ask the usher to give P2224 to the witness or to put it up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Again, Mr. Visnjic, the transcript says: "In paragraph 45 you state that on the 26th of March you arrived at Podujevo, you stayed for two days," now should that be Prolom Banja?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. I have to switch this. Yes, Your Honour, it should be "Prolom Banja."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see paragraph 45 on the screen, that is page 8.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stoparic, I presume you see paragraph 45. The first sentence says: "We were here for two days," and that means in Prolom Banja. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: On the 28th of April -- pardon, March, you were in Podujevo. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It should be correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 62 it is stated that upon your return from Podujevo a part of the group remained at Prolom Banja for five or six days. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the incident in Podujevo, it is true that we spent several days at Prolom Banja.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Then you returned to Sid. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went back to Sid and the others went to their respective houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I had you in mind. Some ten days later, as stated in paragraph 63 of your statement, some Boca's men came for you -- to see you and some other Skorpions, and they told you to gather at the same place as previously. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Those people told me that we were to go again.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: By the way, while you were in Sid for the ten days, were you in Sid or somewhere else, the ten days between your return from Prolom Banja and the moment when you were again taken away by Boca's men?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat his answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry, the interpreter is asking for a repetition of the answer there. What was your answer to that question, Mr. Stoparic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was asked whether I spent the ten days in Sid. I said that I think I spent the whole time in Sid.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Having been assembled, and according to your statement you said it must have been around the 15th or the 16th of April, 1999, you were taken by buses straight to Kosovo Polje in Kosovo. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we went via Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: You spent some time in Kosovo, during which you participated in the operations of driving Albanian or KLA terrorists away. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: You said that on the 1st of May your unit was tasked with taking over a transmitter on top of a mountain guarded by some 50 KLA terrorists. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I could see from the reconnaissance we did the previous day, I was there with some other members of the SAJ, and we thought the number or the figure of their fighters was around that number.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Then you stated the next day, on the 2nd of May, around noon you were shot by a KLA terrorist in the elbow?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: On the same day, you were transported to the hospital around 9.00 p.m. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, around that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: You spent two days at the intensive care unit at the hospital. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Two days later, is it true that a jeep came to pick you up with two people who dropped you off at Banjica in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: How long did you stay at the orthopaedic clinic at Banjica?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not for too long. I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Perhaps to jog your memory, in paragraph 77 you state that your elbow was operated on there, and as far as I understood you received some skin grafts as well. Therefore, my question is: Were you at the military medical academy throughout that time?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean at Banjica? That's not the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was in the hospital all that time. The first operation was done in Pristina right after the wounding. The second one, as far as I remember it, was done by a plastic surgeon and they transplanted some grafts of skin at the orthopaedic clinic at Banjica.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Do you have any sense of the time that you spent at Banjica? Was it until the end of the war or a bit longer or did you leave before the end of the war? Perhaps we could use that as a landmark.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll try to recall that. I was visited at Banjica by some members of the Skorpions, which probably -- or should mean that they had returned by that time from Kosovo. But whether the NATO air-strikes had ceased, well, I don't know. I didn't pay much heed to that. I was dealing with my injuries.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Once discharged from the hospital, I presume you went back home to Sid?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: If I conclude, based on your testimony today, would I be correct that in the period between the 24th of March and the 10th of June, when the war ended, the 10th of June of 1999, you didn't visit the SAJ base at Batajnica?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're absolutely right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Stoparic, am I correct if I conclude, based on your testimony today, that you didn't know what the security system was at the SAJ base at Batajnica between the 24th of March, 1999 until the 10th of June, 1999?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note, as the counsel says.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I know about the security system refers to the period of time when I visited the base.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Would I be correct then to conclude that you don't know whether the military police had any control or check-points in front of the SAJ base between the 24th of March, 1999 until the 10th of June, 1999?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As regards that period, I have no knowledge of that. I don't -- I know when I was there. First you had to go through the military police check-point and then the actual gate of the SAJ base.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: But you don't know it for a fact whether that was indeed so between the 24th of March, 1999 until the 10th of June, 1999. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't know that if I didn't visit the base during that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stoparic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Visnjic. Does that conclude the cross-examination? Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I just have a very few questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Stoparic, when your group from Sid got on the buses to go to Boca's house and then to Kosovo on or around the 24th or 25th of March, 1999, and you were told that you were being taken as a reserve unit of the SAJ, were you taken as a group or individuals, if you understand my question? Was it the Skorpions as your group, or did you get screened person by person to go into the SAJ?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Boca, my then-commander, Slobodan Medic, actually, organised our assembly as a group. I don't see that anyone went there on an individual basis. We went there together, all of us together. But then I'm not quite sure that I absolutely did understand your question. Did you mean whether we went there -- whether we were summoned either officially by post or by courier, or did we just assemble and board buses and then set out towards our destination? No, if that is what you meant. It was on a voluntary basis. We did not receive any such summons in any way.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
