utterances.text: And you were kept together as a group and not dispersed to separate detachments or units?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we kept together as a group.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. From today's questioning -- I think it was Mr. Lukic at page 15, beginning at line 2, he was asking you about the service booklets that you'd gotten that showed you as being members of the MUP of Serbia, and he had a discussion with you about that seemed to be contradictory with what you had said before when you'd asked if a couple of your friends could join. Do you recall that discussion where you said that Srdjan Manojlovic told you they wanted to keep the percentages so that the percentage of members from Republika Srpska and Republika Srpska Krajina were higher than the percentage of members from Serbia? Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you yourself are from Serbia, yes?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So there's no reason that your book shouldn't show you a member from Serbia. Correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No reason whatsoever why my address shouldn't be in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But if your two new friends were to come in, they might change the percentage to higher than they wanted it to be at the time?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see, sir, I would not probably have said anything about this at all, but what surprised me was that whenever I recommended a soldier to be admitted, I was always trusted. So they did admit those soldiers to join. That is why I talked with Manojlovic along those lines, and that is why I transmitted the content of our talks of mine and Manojlovic's talk to you in that way. That is the kind of response I got. And as a matter of fact, he did not admit these two friends of mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And then earlier, when Mr. Lukic was asking you about after the shooting in Podujevo when you Skorpions were put on the bus and returned to Serbia. He asked you if you viewed that as some kind of punishment. I want to ask you: During that time period when you were sent back, did you continue to get paid?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First you asked me whether I considered this to be punishment. I was expecting punishment. I don't understand this about getting a salary. What do you mean? While we are not in the field or during such periods? Can you please clarify for me. Are you referring to the period of ten or 15 days spent at home? Is that the period you are referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I am referring to that. Do you view that as a punishment?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no. I was expecting punishment. It wasn't punishment. I don't see what it is that you're alluding to, that I was sent on leave for ten days, sent home for leave. I was, in fact, expecting a different kind of punishment for the perpetrators and for all of us because we disgraced that unit. You know what it means to disgrace the SAJ?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Was anybody fined, charged a money penalty?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did anybody get demoted?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: How can a reservist be demoted? You can only not call him again. No one was demoted. If what you mean is that they didn't call people again, no. It wasn't the case. Whoever came to the bus would go.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I think you said when you -- when you returned after the 15 days or so, that many of the same Skorpions who had gone with you the first time were in the second group that returned. Correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Including three of the four that you were aware of as being involved in the shooting of those civilians?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I have no further questions of this witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hannis. Mr. Stoparic, that completes your evidence. Thank you for coming to the International Tribunal to give it. You're now free to leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think that we might have a short opportunity for re-cross.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: After re-direct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is this a new form of procedure that we're going to be following? You've had your opportunity to cross-examine. Is there some particular reason why you ought to have another opportunity?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In cases I was before this Tribunal before this case, I always had the opportunity to have a re-cross after re-direct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I've never encountered that -- well, albeit my experience here is limited, but I have neither encountered it in domestic proceedings nor here. But what is it in particular you wish to raise?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That would be the question that regarding this booklet that this witness had, Serbian booklet, because he is from Serbia. I just wanted to clarify whether other members of Skorpions had also Serbian booklets, regardless of the place where they come from. One of the questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do you have any objection to that, Mr. Hannis?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: As long as we make sure we're asking about which ones he knew about and whether he knew about all of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah. Well, we will allow you to ask this question, but bear in mind that this will not be the normal procedure followed here --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I hope that it would --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm sorry?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I hope it would.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Where, for example?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry, is somebody operating you from behind?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, my colleague Ivetic is helping me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I'm certainly not aware of it as being the procedure here. Has someone else got experience of this as the way in which things proceed here? Well, it's -- I can tell you now it's not the way it's going to be proceeding in this court, so you should be careful when you're cross-examining to cross-examine completely. If something in re-examination is raised that is unforeseeable by counsel cross-examining, then you could make a special application to come back. And indeed if Judges, for example, were to ask questions and that was after you had concluded your cross-examination and those raised issues that you thought you ought to have a chance to explore, then you might come back. But in a routine situation like we've just experienced here, that's certainly not the way in which this Tribunal has worked nor is it the way in which this particular court will work. But on this occasion, since you misunderstood the position, I will allow you to ask the question you wish to ask.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I just want to draw your attentions to cases of Foca, Omarska --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, before you -- Mr. Fila seems to wish to intervene now.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Mr. President, I just wish to be useful. We have had such cases in our practice, especially because in contrast to you questions [as interpreted] from England do not ask too many questions; continental judges in Serbia, either ones asking the questions mainly, not the Prosecutor and the Defence. So it's very difficult for us to adapt when we come here. In the Omarska case, all the Judges did the asking and then we also followed with our questions. The president of the court, Cassese, allowed the defence counsel one question each after the re-direct. So we have had such cases in our practice. That is my personal view. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, thank you, Mr. Fila. Rule 85(B) of the Rules of Procedure says clearly: "Examination-in-chief, cross-examination, and re-examination shall be allowed in each case," and nothing could be clearer than that in my view. Anything else that has occurred has been an indulgence outwith the Rules.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's consistent with my limited experience in the Tribunal in the Krajisnik case. There was direct, there was cross, there was re-direct. And then if the Judges had questions that opened up something new, then both parties were allowed to ask additional questions, or in the event that on re-direct there was something brand new that went sort of beyond the scope of the cross-exam, then certainly they were entitled to ask about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All of that is clear. Thank you, Mr. Hannis. Anyway, Mr. Lukic, carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, I'll have only one question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stoparic, are you aware of the fact, or do you know what kinds of military service booklets the other members of the Skorpions had and was it connected with the places from which they came?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see that there is a misunderstanding here. I said simply if you were from Serbia your address was there. I didn't say Serbian in the sense of Serbia proper. You had your address and it was written whether it --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who actually issued those booklets?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Manojlovic brought them. As far as I can remember, they had been made in Vukovar, and it has something to do with the Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Anything arising, Mr. Hannis?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, Mr. Stoparic, that does now complete your evidence. Thank you for coming to the Tribunal to give it. You're now free to leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good-bye. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, before we go on to the next witness, one matter I'd like to put on the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, the unredacted version of the diagram.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's attached to his statement is P2229, and we would ask that that be entered under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, that will happen. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. That's all I had in connection with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, I have something to ask you, Mr. Hannis, before we proceed. The Trial Chamber would welcome clarification of the purpose of the evidence relating Podujevo. I notice that that atrocity is not specified at all in the indictment. Why is that? And in light of that, what is the purpose of the evidence about that?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think the evidence concerning Podujevo came to the attention of our office after the original indictment was put together. It was not included. Why it was not amended later on to include, I cannot say. Part of the reason for this evidence, though, Your Honour, is to show the nature of the units involved, and it relates partly to argument about failure to punish or lack of punishment. You will recall in our pre-trial brief and some of our prior pleadings we talked about one of the reasons that goes to the knowledge or intent of these accused relates to the fact that they used some units for whom they had an awareness, had engaged in illegal or criminal acts in prior combat activities in the Balkans before that time period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But that can only be relevant if the event itself somehow or other is to be the subject of a decision by the Tribunal at the end of -- by the Trial Chamber at the end of the evidence. Now, are you going to be asking us to make a decision that there was an atrocity in Podujevo that we should just somehow or other filter into the indictment, it never having been mentioned there?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we're not asking you to make a specific finding about Podujevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I'm now not clear about its purpose. To show the nature of the units involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The Skorpions were with -- 50 per cent of these volunteers without any training who were --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. But are you going to tell -- is there going to be evidence of the Skorpions committing some of the atrocities that are in the indictment?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, you heard evidence from this witness that he was involved in operations in the Jezerce area in Suva Reka municipality and in Strpce. And some of our evidence is about the removal of Kosovo Albanians from the Suva Reka area. I think you'll see some documentary evidence relating specifically to operations in that area. We think it also goes to our allegations about joint operations between the VJ and the MUP, which will be in that documentary evidence. Your Honour, if you still have concerns about it, what I would propose is that you delay a decision on that until you've heard further evidence in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm not -- there's no decision to be made, Mr. Hannis. It's to help the Chamber understand why we hear evidence about something that each one of us instantly thinks: That should be part of the indictment. Why is it not? It seems such a simple matter when somebody speaks so plainly about an event that you would expect it to be in the indictment. And I'm finding it difficult to understand why it's not.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's a historical matter that relates to a time in this case before I was on this case. I can't answer those questions, not at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It -- yeah. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But our indictment does allege this programme of deportations and killings that were done which added to the campaign of terror resulted in those people fleeing. A part of our argument is that they fled not because of NATO bombing but because of the activities of the Serb forces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I understand that. But, you know, especially when this indictment was amended and there was -- it was very -- there was keen debate about how much specification was required, you know, one has to be concerned about this sort of omission which also -- and this particular evidence, I'm speaking obviously from my own background knowledge in another case, but this particular evidence and whether it should be admitted or not was a big issue in the Milosevic trial. And as you know, a decision was -- or you may or may not know, a decision was made not to allow re-opening of the case to allow this among other evidence in.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I do know that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, the other matter I want to deal with at this stage is this: I indicated yesterday that we would have some preliminary discussions of the status of As Seen, As Told. And as a result of that, we have decided to order the Prosecution to make certain further submissions, to which the Defence will have the opportunity to respond. But we are not asking the Defence to take the initiative because these are confined to certain specific subjects, and it will be adequate for our purposes and to reflect the interests of the Defence if they respond to the Prosecution filing on the matter. And there are three areas arising out of the evidence of Ms. Mitchell on -- in relation to As Seen, As Told on which we require further submission from the Prosecution. Number one is: Which parts of the report does the Prosecution accept should not be part of the evidence in the case? Secondly, we wish expansion so far as possible upon the submissions already made about the reasons for completion of the forms which are the foundation of the report. And that is the forms about human rights abuses and the forms about the movement of persons within Kosovo and also over the border into Albania and Macedonia. And in particular, these submissions should deal with the question whether one of the reasons for provision -- or indeed the reason for the provision of the information was to transmit it to the Prosecution for the purposes of litigation before the Tribunal. Now, the request for this second submission arises out of reference to the Appeals Chamber decision in Milosevic, which was on the 30th of September, 2002. The third matter on which further submission is ordered is in relation to how the Prosecution envisaged the content of the report being used by the Chamber in its deliberations on the substantive issues in this case, and that should be illustrated by specific examples which relate the use that might be made of the report to other evidence that you anticipate being presented, whether it's accepted or not. Let's assume for the moment it will be evidence in the case. The various areas that Mr. Stamp suggested yesterday would benefit from this report, while it wouldn't provide a basis for any finding in relation to any specific offence, it could assist the Trial Chamber in corroborating crime scenes. Well, we have difficulty understanding that submission and would like it to be expanded. We would like you to expand how it would assist our deliberations on the question of whether conduct was widespread and systematic. We require expansion on how you consider it can assist us on the question of notice to the accused of events within Kosovo. And lastly, how it might assist us on an analysis of the background to the conflict, which -- I think that exhausts the various ways in which Mr. Stamp submitted it could assist the Trial Chamber. Now, Mr. Stamp, timing, we would like this done fairly quickly. Do you have any specific request so far as time is concerned?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I would answer some time tomorrow, any time convenient to the Court tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah. I'm seeking written --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Oh, written submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- submissions. So if a week is what --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: A week --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- you would wish, then we'll say next Friday, which is the 21st, and that would allow us to give probably ten days, I think to be fair to the Defence. I'll allow them over the weekend as well. So that would be the 28th, 29th, 30th, 31st of July for the Defence response, rather than the normal 14 days. I think so that prior to the end of the recess this is dealt with and staff can work on it for the assistance of the Chamber on their return. Thank you. Now, you may care to note these concerns in relation to the person I anticipate is the next witness, and you may, therefore, care to address in the oral evidence, at least to some extent, the second issue that I've raised with you. Now, who is the next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The next witness is Fred Abrahams. But before we get him, may I just ask for clarification. I'm not sure if I heard Your Honour correctly in respect to the second question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You said, I think, reasons for the completion forms?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. Why were these forms being completed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In other words, why was this system established to collect material? Was it for the purpose of prosecution before the Tribunal? And if not, what was the purpose? And obviously, you'll have to have regard to the evidence that the witness gave, but if there's other assistance that you feel you can properly give to the Chamber, then you should give it. Now, can we bring in Mr. Abrahams now?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Abrahams.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Could I invite you, please, to make the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Mr. Abrahams, could you please state your full name.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: Frederick C. Abrahams.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What's your present occupation or position?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: I'm a senior emergencies researcher at Human Rights Watch.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And did you give and attest to a declaration or a statement at OTP on May 30, 2002?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And subsequently, on the 11th of July, 2006, you gave another statement that you signed?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And you reviewed these statements, did you?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And are they true and accurate to the extent that they are -- if you were asked the same questions again, now, would your answers remain the same?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: Yes, I would, and I will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, what are the exhibit numbers of these statements?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And the dates are 30 May 2002 and 11th July.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Actually, the -- by way of clarification, the document of the 30th of May, 2002 is a composite of three statements. This was, in fact, his declaration or a preparation made under Rule 92 bis. There had been an intention in the past to seek to introduce his evidence under Rule 92 bis. So P2228 could be described as his 92 bis statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, among the matters which you discussed in your statement was an investigation in respect to human rights issues in the Drenica region in September of 1998?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you personally go to Drenica in that period?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you go alone or did you go with colleagues?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: I was with one colleague, Mr. Peter Bouckaert --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could you spell his surname, please.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: B-o-u-c-k-a-e-r-t.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: About when did you arrive in that area?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: We arrived in Kosovo in approximately mid-September, but our specific investigations in Drenica commenced in the end of that month, around September 25th and 26th.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And what were your observations when you arrived in the Drenica area?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: At the time there was an ongoing offensive by Serbian and Yugoslav forces in the Drenica area, in fact throughout Kosovo. And we were denied access on numerous occasions into the Drenica valley, blocked by -- by security forces. But --

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Sepenuk.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: I just want to get a clarification here. As I understand it, this event, September of 1998, pre-dates the indictment period, the charging period. And I'd like to know what the particular relevance is at this time -- at least I would ask for the Prosecution's explanation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, without having every page of the indictment at my finger-tips, I'm pretty sure this is referred to in the indictment, specifically towards -- if you go to the general allegations at the end, I think it's in one of these paragraphs. Mr. Stamp, can you help us with the paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]. It's probably paragraph 99. I know it's -- it certainly is discussed -- or at least aspects of the evidence, it certainly is discussed in the pre-trial brief at paragraph 95. Or paragraph 92 of the pre-trial brief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, what we have in the indictment in 95 is around 5 and 6 August operations were conducted in the area of Drenica, Junik and Jablanica. And then by the end of September, forces of the FRY and Serbia had shelled and bombed down about half of the villages in Decani.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: But unless I'm missing a point, Your Honour, it does pre-date the inception of the alleged joint criminal enterprise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah. Well, that issue has been explored in detail already, Mr. Sepenuk, and these averments have been held to be relevant, at least in the context of the indictment amendment process. And you'll see that there are averments from about the position from February 1998 onwards, and therefore evidence will be led covering that whole period. And at the moment it seems to me that this is close enough to what's in the indictment to allow the evidence to proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: That's a decision that's already been taken by the Chamber, I take it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Oh, yeah, you can see -- well, there was exception taken to these paragraphs of the indictment, but they were allowed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I just -- just before you do go on, I'm actually having difficulty with this package of material you've given me in hard copy, which is easier to work with I think in the context of these bulky statements. There's something that was signed on the 11th of July which you've referred to, and that is a statement extending to 19 paragraphs. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's then followed by -- this must be -- yeah, this is the Serbian version and then there's a 92 bis document which seems to rope in three separate statements?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. So where do we go to find the evidence that you're now leading?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In respect to Drenica?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Which is why I am covering it orally. The statement does not completely cover that part. It refers to a report, and there are some photographs which are attached or which are indicated to be exhibits, which the Prosecution would like him to identify. And those photographs relate to this incident.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And the date of that?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The date of the?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, it's -- the -- between the 26th and the 29th of September, 1998.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And that's not referred to in the indictment?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: It is in the indictment and in the pre-trial brief. I'm saying in the statement --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, where is it in the indictment? I mean, I thought -- I found it for August, but this is something you say was three specific days or four specific days in September.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The last sentence in paragraph 95 of the indictment, which I'll just read. "On the 26th of September in the course of an anti-terrorist operation in and around" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So that's what we're about to look at?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So who what time did you and your colleague arrive in the area?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: The first day that we entered was September 26th, the first day we entered into Drenica. We visited the villages of Plocica and we saw what we considered to be the systematic destruction of civilian property. And we also saw in the distance the burning of another village called Gornje Obrinje. We saw the smoke rising from that area, took photographs of the village. But we did our investigations only in Plocica on that day as well as another village, Mlecane nearby, where we observed Serbian policemen in blue uniforms carrying what looked like personal goods out of a private home, which we considered to be evidence of looting. But we did not actually get into the Gornje Obrinje village until September 29th. We heard about an incident in the village the previous night, on September 28th, where reports had reached Pristina, where we were staying, that a family of ethnic Albanians had been killed near their home.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What is the family name; do you remember?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: The family name was Delija.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you spell that, please.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: Well, there are various spellings but most common is D-e-l-i-j-a.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So you went to Gornje Obrinje on the 29th?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What were your observations there in that area?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: When my colleague and I arrived in Gornje Obrinje, villagers were in the process of removing bodies from the forest. They were carrying three young children out from a wooded area to a nearby field for burial. And seven other bodies still lay in the forest, most of them in a small gully that ran up from a path. They were all women and children. The youngest was an 18-month-old baby, and the villagers were in the process of taking these bodies out from the area so they could be -- so they could be buried.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, did you receive information as to how these persons died?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: My colleague and I divided tasks. Mr. Bouckaert took photographs of the area while I began to interview the family members and neighbours in the area, and we commenced an in-depth investigation that lasted -- we returned, actually, to Kosovo again in December to continue the investigation, so it was a matter of weeks, in which -- during which we interviewed dozens of individuals with knowledge of the incident. And our conclusion was that these were civilians, that they were hiding in the forest because of ongoing fighting in the village between the Kosovo Liberation Army and Serbian security forces. There was fighting going on in that village --

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Sepenuk.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: I think we're in the area again of conclusions. And I would -- I would very much object to these conclusions. I suppose the witness can -- can describe what he did and I suppose also under the rules of the Tribunal, although I still think we would like to have a continuing objection to what's obviously hearsay, regardless -- I realise we have 89(C), but -- and he can testify to that, I say, over our objection. But I do -- but we do object, at least the Ojdanic Defence team, I'm assuming the other Defence teams, object to any conclusions that this witness draws from these observations, for the same reasons that we've previously expressed with the testimony of Ms. Mitchell. I think the fact that he was personally there does not make a difference. He's still making conclusions, and I don't think he's got a right to do that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Lukic Defence team would concur and join in the objection. And we would point out that, again, as with the objections to the Mitchell report this witness seems to be making legal conclusions as to specific matters that are the crux of the case. I believe the witness in the transcript testified to certain actions being systematic. I believe that those are the crux of the case and, you know, he's making legal conclusions based upon that. So we would again reiterate the same objections we raised with respect to the testimony and the exhibits in the -- for Ms. Mitchell.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, we join the objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the Lazarevic Defence joins the objection as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm interested in the following, Your Honours, whether we need to stand up one by one every time that we concur and join, or perhaps maybe we can do that in a written form. In any case, we second our colleague's opinion, but I just want to be instructed for the future. Should we all nod at the same time or how should we go about it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think it is important that you confirm that you are supporting an objection. It's all you need to say if you're happy with the argument that's already been advanced. And I see Mr. Aleksic joins in to complete the hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely so, Your Honours. We join the argument.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Your response, Mr. Stamp?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: To a significant degree, my response would be the same response in respect to the arguments raised yesterday in respect to hearsay evidence. It is admissible --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, it's certainly admissible. That's -- the objection, though, this time is that what the witness is doing is giving us his conclusions rather than telling us the facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. If I could put the question this way. Did the witnesses that he interviewed tell him what happened and what did they tell him happened?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah. But if you think that makes a difference, I'm afraid it doesn't, because it -- if you're going to ask the content, then that's different, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah. Well, if you wish to withdraw the previous question -- well, it really wasn't the question. It was an objection to the answer which I think we should treat as an objection to the line which sought conclusions from the witness. And if you want to approach it another way, we'll allow you to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Just for the record, although this is in the 89(F) statement and I did not want to ask too much that was already before the Court in the statements, may I just ask for the record --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I thought you said this wasn't and that was why you were when I asked you --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No, no, what I was about to ask about what he was doing there then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What was your role and function in Kosovo in 1998.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: Yes. My role was to monitor and document violations of human rights law and international humanitarian law.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: On behalf of?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: On behalf of Human Rights Watch.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And Human Rights Watch is?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: Human Rights Watch is a non-governmental, non-profit organisation that operates in more than 70 countries around the world to document and publicise violations of the law and to advocate on behalf of victims and for international justice and accountability.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, as a Human Rights Watch monitor, you interviewed these villagers. What did they tell you happened to these people whose bodies you saw?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: We interviewed more than two dozen individuals in relation to this incident in Gornje Obrinje. We always conduct our interviews in one-on-one settings. They are lengthy processes to obtain detailed information that we can corroborate, and in this case we heard from the witnesses that fighting had taken place between the KLA and Serbian security forces. We later learned that some Serbian police had died as well. But this family from -- the Delija family, they had fled their homes during the shelling by Serbian forces to seek protection in the woods. And we spoke with individuals who then first found their bodies because other people fled at that time. And according to three witnesses we interviewed separately who discovered the bodies, these people had been -- had been killed while hiding in the -- in this area.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Killed by?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: According to these witnesses, they were killed by the Serbian security forces that were active in the Drenica valley. There were, if I'm not mistaken, 14 people killed in the forest and 21 from the family in total. So five were killed in other areas around the village and the family compound.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did Human Rights Watch publish a report in respect of your findings?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: We did. We published a very detailed report, a small book, that took many weeks to research and it includes all our detailed findings with footnotes of the specific interviews and any secondary sources that are cited.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What's the name of that publication?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: A Week of Terror in Drenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: About when was that published; do you remember?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: I believe that was January, perhaps February 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, when you say "published," published in what sense. How was it disseminated, can you remember specifically to who or to which organisations?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: As is our normal procedure, Human Rights Watch publishes a printed copy which gets disseminated widely to the media, to governments, as well as universities, libraries, and other institutions. The material is also posted on the web site, as well as sent around by fax -- at least the press release and sometimes the summary of the report are sent by fax and e-mail. And the organisation maintained a very lengthy list of contacts within Yugoslavia that included all of the relevant government offices which received this report and other reports we published subsequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honour, this report is referred to and discussed in his evidence, his 89 bis -- his 89(F) evidence, so I will not go into it anymore, but I could point to that it's Exhibit P -- P441.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Which page of the statement is it on?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Page 4 of the statement, paragraph -- in the Exhibit P2227, that is paragraph 19. And in the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah. Is it referred to any of the other statements?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, it's referred to in the other statement at page 6 where there is a discussion, that is P2228. It's referred there in -- at page 6 where there is the discussion as to the method in which the evidence was collected and the analysis was drawn --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Page 6 of 19? Is that the one with 19 pages?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Page 6 of -- yes, the one of 2nd of March.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I don't --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I should use the P number, page 6 of P2228.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, that's not easy because 2228 has several bits to it, doesn't it? It's got three separate statements that all have their own pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Okay. I think we'll have to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There doesn't seem to be separate numbering of that particular exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: We were using the e-court numbering. So page 6 is the number in e-court. I'll get the ERN number shortly so you could --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Let's have it on the screen then.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. P2228.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Page 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I could also indicate, if it might be of assistance, the front page of the 92 bis statement is page 1, that is K0225261. It's page 1 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, two matters. One question for the witness, first of all. You said that 14 people were found in the forest and that there were five killed elsewhere, but we have a total of 21.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, you're right. I'm sorry, Your Honour, that's my calculating error. There were -- there were seven people in the forest when we arrived, and the -- I believe it's five people were killed in other parts of the village. And the remaining had already been taken out; in other words, when we arrived, the family was in the process of taking the bodies out of the forest to -- for burial in a nearby field.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. And my question for you, Mr. Stamp, is the use to which this information should be put in connection with the indictment, is it simply a question of notice?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: It is primarily a question of notice. It primarily goes to the issues that will arise under Rule 73.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: May I just make an inquiry. There are many attachments to the report which are referred to in the 82 bis [sic] statement. I don't intend, except if you require, that I ask him to do what is already done in the statement because I was hoping that we would not have to use that much time in-chief so that we could ensure that he's finished.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I think the answer to your question depends on the purpose of the evidence. If it's simply a question of publications which were brought to the attention of government authorities in Yugoslavia, that's one thing. If you're asking us to look at the facts and make findings in fact from what's declared as an account of fact in the report, that's another matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You then, I think, need to raise each one and give us at least an indication of what it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And I will do so even if that is already done in the documentary evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think it has to be done here because I think I've indicated that we don't want -- simply want things thrown at us and left to sort it out. We want your guidance on how to make use of the material which is being provided, and that means some indication of the general nature of a report and the purpose for which it might be used as part of the evidence in this case. We don't have the documents, they're in the e-court, so we can't deduce simply from a reference to the document in this written statement what it is and what its relevance might be.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You said that it took once -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Carry on, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You said either yourself or Mr. -- or your colleague --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Bouckaert.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: -- took some photographs. If you saw those photographs, would you be able to identify them now?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: Yes, I would.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we, with your permission, put on the screen, the e-court screen, P642.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Abrahams, were they part of the report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What is that photograph depicting?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: This photograph depicts two children of the Delija family who are being carried out of the forest for burial.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And could we quickly move on because we might have quite a few documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we have a look at P702. Could we rotate -- yeah, right, thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And what does this one depict?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: This photo was taken on September 26th in the village of Plocica. It shows a distraught villager in front of a food warehouse. I inspected that building, and it contained melons and other food items that were obviously burning and was typical of the destruction we saw that day in the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we have a look at P679.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could you --

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: This photo is also from the forest outside Gornje Obrinje depicting one of the children from the family, which is how we -- how we found the bodies when we arrived.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, would you find a suitable time to interrupt please, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: This would be a convenient time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, we'll break now and we'll resume at five past 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Could we move on now to P653.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I gather there are certain problems with this document in e-court, and it would be helpful if you had hard copies. Is that easy or difficult?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: It is a photograph. I'm not sure if I have hard copies. There is a black and white copy. I'm wondering if it's a problem that might be resolved by tomorrow? Maybe I can defer that one --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Does it matter greatly that we see all the photographs when we can see them attached to the report?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No, I think one could -- I'm not sure if that particular one is attached to the report, but they are referred to in the statement, his statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, the witness told me in an answer to a question I asked that the photographs were part of the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Were -- very well --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I mean, I would have to -- all of the photographs we have seen thus far are in the report. I'm not certain whether the next one is.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you said that the human rights reports were published and disseminated to various persons, including government organisations. Within the FRY, what government departments or organs or persons were these reports sent to directly that you know?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: Typically these reports were sent to the government institutions and agencies, bodies, that relate to either Kosovo or matters of justice. So specifically in this case, it would have been the Presidency of Serbia and the Federal Presidency of Yugoslavia, the Republican and Federal Ministries of Justice and Interior, as well as the Yugoslav army.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did where do you also have mailing list, an e-mailing list?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And had did this list include persons who occupied high office in the Yugoslav government and the Serbian government?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And if you could, in a sentence or two, elaborate on disseminated in the media. When you say "disseminated in the media," like what media?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: The organisation maintains a large collection of media contacts, so our statements are sent to the wire services, Reuters, Associated Press, Agence France-Presse, as well as the major newspapers in -- all around the world, English language and otherwise. And we also made a particular effort to distribute to the media in the countries where we operate, so in this case Yugoslavia. And with regards to Kosovo, both to the Serbian-language and Albanian-language media.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, you said there were other reports that were prepared by Human Rights Watch in respect to the affairs or the events that were taking place in Kosovo. I'd like to refer you to another one of these reports, and that is Exhibit P388 entitled "Kosovo Human Rights Watch flash number 31, rape of ethnic Albanian women in the Suva Reka municipality."

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: For the assistance of the Court, if it might assist. This is discussed in his statement P2228 at pages 6 and 7 -- e-court pages 6 and 7, and pages 22 to 23.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: This is a Human Rights Watch flash. Could you tell us briefly what that was and what was the methodology in preparing and sending out a flash?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: When the NATO bombing of Yugoslavia commenced in March 1999, we immediately mobilised a research team to the borders of -- of Kosovo. We were not allowed entry into Kosovo at that time. We also deemed it too dangerous. So our researchers were on the borders of Albania and Macedonia to interview the ethnic Albanian refugees who were fleeing and being, in our view, according to their testimony, being expelled from the province. And we had someone on the ground in both Albania and Macedonia throughout the period of the NATO bombing. During -- and we produced during that time what we called Human Rights Watch flash. It was a way to disseminate information in a more realtime and rapid manner, quicker than our normal reports allow because the information was so fast-flowing. We wanted to disseminate what we considered to be very serious violations. So this particular flash was produced in April. I was on the ground in northern Albania, the town of Kukes at the time with a colleague Joanne Mariner. She is the primary researcher who located the women who gave very detailed and consistent testimony about the sexual abuse they experienced in their village near Suva Reka. I was present at the time and consulted with my colleague during her research, but she conducted the interviews, due to the necessity of having a woman researcher interview female victims on a sensitive matter. But I was involved further by -- in the editing and preparation of this particular flash number 31.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And was that disseminated in the same manner that you described earlier in respect to human rights reports generally?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: Yes, it was. In particular, the flashes were disseminated by e-mail. And if I could just add one quick point.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: These flashes and all the information we collected during the period of the NATO bombing, we then followed up on once we were allowed into Kosovo after the NATO bombing had stopped. And we returned to this village to collect further information. And based on our investigations there and more interviews, we confirmed that the facts, as we had obtained them in northern Albania, were consistent -- we obtained the consistent information, based on the further investigations.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I can have a brief objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: -- to this particular document. I believe that Mr. Stamp indicated that this material was being brought in for the purposes of establishing prior notice on the part of the accused --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, that applied to the earlier one. He hasn't said anything about the purpose of this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I would be willing to inquire about that insofar as the date of this document appears to be 2000. It's updated on February 22nd, 2000. So if that is indeed the purpose for which this document is being presented, I would object on those grounds. And again, if it's being presented for the purpose of proving the direct crime that is alleged, then obviously my standing objection is relative to the violation of Rule 92 bis, et cetera, would stand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The dates at the top of the document -- perhaps a couple questions to the witness might clarify the issue in respect to the dates.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You see the first line of the document, it says updated on 27 -- I beg your pardon, "updated on February 22, 2000." And then in the third line you see, "New York, April 28, 1999." Can you explain the meaning of those two dates, please.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: The date April 28th refers to the day and time when this document was made public from our offices in New York.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes. And the date above?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: The February 22nd?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: My belief, but I am not certain at this point, but my assumption is this is based on the subsequent research we conducted after entering Kosovo and were able to elaborate on this. But honestly speaking, I'm not sure what that updated date refers to. I'm sorry. I could probably check it if it's necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: But in respect to the core allegation of rape in Suva Reka, the flash was issued on the 28th of April, 1999?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, is that an acknowledgment from you that the purpose of this again is notice?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And you'll appreciate the difficulty, of course, is that we don't know what the notice was on the 28th of April, 1999, because this one is dated the 22nd of February, 2000.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, there is an issue, clearly, but the evidence of the witness is that the core allegation of rape in that district in that area which is on the indictment. It was disseminated then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In paragraph 19 of the last statement that you gave, that is P2227 for the record, and at paragraph 19 you refer to a document called "a week of" -- withdrawn. I'm on the wrong document. At paragraph 18 you refer to a document called "human rights" -- "Humanitarian Law Violations in Kosovo." And that for the record is P437. And you say that you are the author of the report and it was based on a search you conducted in the field between May and September 1998. And in that statement as well at paragraph 5 you refer to a document -- a report called "Kosovo: Rape as a Weapon of Ethnic Cleansing," and that for the record is P386. You said that you participate -- you jointly conducted interviews with some of the general witnesses, such as doctors and human rights activists, and you also edited the report.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And the last report I wish to refer you to before I ask some general questions about these reports is referred to at paragraph 17 of your statement, and it is entitled "Under Orders: War Crimes in Kosovo." And for the record that is P438. Would you say you are the coordinator of that work and you are the principal author of this document?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: That's correct. It was a collaborative effort, but I was the primary coordinator of the project.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In the collection of information that was used for the preparation of these reports, how many staff did you have available to you?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: Are you referring to any report in particular or the reports in general?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The reports in general. If they are different, please tell us; if they -- logistics are different, let us know.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: They are different. For example, the report humanitarian law violations in Kosovo was researched solely by me and written by me but then went through a rigorous editing process, as is Human Rights Watch standard procedure, so that at least two and usually three different editors review the material before publication. The report "rape as a tactic of ethnic cleansing," if that's the exact title, was researched by an expert in women's rights and sexual violence, a woman named Martina Vandenberg with assistance from a second Human Rights Watch researcher, Joanne Mariner, and myself. But as I mentioned before, the interviews with women were conducted solely by Ms. Vandenberg, while I participated in the general interviews with doctors rather than specific witnesses. And I also edited that report and gave Ms. Vandenberg guidance with regards to the proper context in which those violations took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What is the date of publication of that last report you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: If my memory serves me well, it was --

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: -- summer of 1999, but perhaps I'm mistaken.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, again on this particular exhibit the date is March 2000, Kosovo rape as a weapon of ethnic cleansing. I submit if it's being presented for notice it's improper. So perhaps the Prosecution can clarify for what purposes this document is being tendered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: May I just -- may I with your permission just check for the date?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I move on to the next document, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You're not able to assist us if --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The date is correct, so I will not press that one any further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The date of Human Rights Watch report entitled "human rights violations in Kosovo," the date of its publication was October 1998.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: I think that's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we have a look at P437, just to verify that date for the record. P437 is e-court page 3. That's the page. Could we enlarge that page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You see there the first line of that page?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So you will agree with me that that was published in October 1998 by Human Rights Watch?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: Yes, I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And disseminated in the same way you indicated before?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: That's correct. If I -- may I add one note?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: In addition to notification, we also took efforts to obtain the views of the Serbian and Yugoslav government. So during my research for this specific report in the spring of 1998 I met the representative of the Serbian Ministry of Information in Kosovo, Mr. Bosko Drobnjak, to ask him about some of the allegations we had heard and get the government's opinion. And following the mission, I submitted a long list of questions to various government officials in Belgrade, again asking for their comment on -- on a range of topics from government abuses against ethnic Albanians as well as KLA abuses against ethnic Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Sepenuk.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: The witness is talking about letters he sent to various individuals, but I've heard no testimony that letters were sent to any of the six men sitting behind me or that any of these individuals discussed the matter with any of the six men sitting behind me. Perhaps the Prosecution intends to establish that, but absent that kind of line of evidence I fail to see the relevance of this testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, this sort of thing is something you can explore if you feel it will help in cross-examination. And if it's left too vague, then it's not going to be very substantial evidence against you. But we have already had reference to the very first document which was explored, A Week of Terror in Drenica, was submitted to a number of government offices, including the VJ. So I don't think it's the right to say that there's no evidence so far of anything being submitted to an office that might be relevant to any of the accused. But I don't think it's a fundamental matter that rules the evidence out. It's all a question of what it amounts to at the end of the day, and your comment is one that may well be a valid comment when making final submissions. So I repel that objection and invite you to carry on, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That brings me to the matter of letters. Did the organisation Human Rights Watch send letters of protest about human rights -- about allegations of human rights violations or inquiries in respect to alleged human rights violations to the relevant organs of government of the FRY or Serbia?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: Yes, we did. I would qualify those letters as letters of inquiry.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If I could just interrupt for a moment, Your Honour, since we're passing on the letters, have we -- I don't see whether we've already discussed the exhibit Under Orders which we did have an objection to as well, since the copyright date is October 2001. Just for the record, sorry to interrupt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There was no objection taken to Under Orders. Are you now taking an objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I did not notice we had already discussed that one, Your Honour. If it's being presented for the purpose of notice, it's well after the events alleged in the indictment, so I don't see how it could possibly do so, just not been able to open that exhibit up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: It is presented for the purposes of notice to a limited degree, but for all other reasons that the report As Seen, As Told was presented. And I would ask --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: If its date is as stated, which was 2001 I think, then -- is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour, October 2001, this is on -- this is page 5 of exhibit -- of Exhibit P438, if you need --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The report itself can't be submitted for notice.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: As I say, it's a limited degree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, no, no, to a limited degree. I mean, if it's 2001, it's not at all, surely.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In the text of the report it's conceded that the report was published in -- I can't recall the precise date, but certainly after the events that we are speaking of. But in the text, in the body of the report itself, it refers to complaints that they were making before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's a separate matter, but that's something you're now turning to. So notice is resolved so far as the ultimate document is concerned. What else have you to say on it?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, if he's indicated that he's presenting it for the same reasons as the report As Seen, As Told of the OSCE, I think we would reiterate the same objections we had at that time to the extent that the report purports to include statements of individuals who are alleged to be witnesses who are, as far as I can tell, not giving sworn testimony pursuant to 92 bis. If need be, I can prepare a written submission --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, no, I think it's adequate that you indicate that you take the same objection in general terms as you took before. Because it can't be explored in detail until we've heard the evidence of the witness. The decision we would inevitably make would be to reserve the question pending the examination and cross-examination of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I would agree --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And once that -- the situation is clear, then now that you've made it plain that you oppose the admission of the document, then we will have to address that issue in the light of the evidence and your later submissions.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And I can indicate to other counsel that they will have the opportunity, if they wish, to take the same point once the evidence is complete. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'd like to move you quickly through some of those letters that you referred to.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we have a look at P546, please, could it be put on the e-court screen. Could we pan out a little bit so we could -- could we move to the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you know --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you know --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we pan down to the bottom of the page, please, or scroll down, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: This is a letter sent by Holly Cartner, the -- or signed by Holly Cartner, the executive director of the Europe and Central Asia Division of Human Rights Watch. Can you say who drafted this letter?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: I drafted this letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And this letter was in respect to?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: This letter was to obtain information from, in this case, minister Sokolovic, in preparation of our report on Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we move on to P543 -- sorry, P545. Could we go on to the next page, please. May I just confer just for a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And this is another letter dated July 20, 1998, to the Serbian secretary for information to Mr. Aleksandar Vucic.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: Vucic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And this was in order to achieve what?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: This was also to obtain information and the government's views in preparation for our report. The particular questions to Mr. Vucic, Minister Sokolovic and the others varied somewhat, depending on their positions in government.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we have a look at P543.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could you tell us about this very quickly, please.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: This is also a letter to get the government's views in preparation for our report.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: P544, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And this one, what is this one? Could you please move to the next page.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: This is the cover sheet, and the subsequent letter that was sent to the Vojska Jugoslavija, the Yugoslav army.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: P542, could we have a look at that, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And could you tell us about this one very briefly, please.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: This is also a letter to prepare our report addressed to the Serbian minister of the interior, Minister Stojiljkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And P541.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is a similar letter for your report addressed to Minister Knezevic, the Yugoslav minister of justice.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And the last one that we have is P540. Could we have a look at that, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the same letter addressed to the Serbian minister of justice.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The addressees of these letters that you have seen were also among the addressees of the various reports that you prepared and published. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Were the terms of these letters different from one another or are they all identical?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The general framework is the same, but the specific questions varied slightly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we move now to P438, the report entitled "under orders, war crimes in Kosovo."

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You say that you are the principal author of the document?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we have a look at page 4 to 5 of the document in e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is that 4 and 5 or 45?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Page 4 first. And I'll find the -- I think the language on the B/C/S version is page -- I beg your pardon, the page on the B/C/S version is page 3. Are we on page 3? Sorry, on page 4 in the English version. I'm sorry. I have it erroneously here as page 4, but we really need to go to page 19 in the e-court version. And in the B/C/S version it is 11. The report, Your Honours, I think is made available. Can I just read a small passage from it while it's being found?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, you've --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Oh, it's there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You've got it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That part of the report refers to the purpose of the report, and I am going to ask that you elaborate upon the purpose for which Human Rights Watch set out to prepare this report. But I'll just read this section first. It says: "First, it is crucial to provide a historical record. Along with the other reports published thus far, under orders: War crimes in Kosovo will hopefully help future generations to understand better both the conflict and the region. Second, the evidence presented here will be of assistance to war crimes investigators in putting together cases against the Serbian and Yugoslav leadership, as well as against members of the KLA. Assigning individual accountability can help dispel the notion of collective guilt. Lastly, some sectors of Serbian society have expressed interest in evaluating the past. This report might assist that process by providing facts and analysis." Can you elaborate a little upon that in respect to the reasons why Human Rights Watch engaged in preparing this report?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: Human Rights Watch was active in Kosovo documenting human rights abuses since 1990, so we felt a responsibility to present our findings in a comprehensive fashion, which is why Under Orders has substantial background sections. We also felt that publishing this material would contribute to a public debate internationally, but very important for us was inside Yugoslavia, to push aside the rhetoric and established fact. And also as a contribution to international justice, which is firmly within our mandate as an organisation, striving to improve procedures of accountability. So it was a very important objective for us to assist the process of investigations, both in domestic war crimes trials and also international tribunals.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can I ask you, Mr. Abrahams, what use you envisaged a Prosecutor making of the material you gathered?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Firstly, to provide a context, a historical background, a political framework in which the Kosovo conflict could be better understood.
