Secondly, to present the various violations as we documented them so that investigators would have an image of the patterns of the chronologies, as well as the specific cases, essentially as leads. So investigators can pursue on their own the specific villages or the particular violations that they deemed to be of value.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That suggests to me that you envisaged -- your very use of the expression "as leads" suggests to me that you expect the Prosecutor's investigators to go and obtain their own evidence, guided by your initial inquiry.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw my job as facilitating that process or my work was -- was a contribution that would facilitate the investigations by pointing in the right direction through the publication of our reports.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: I have also a question. Excuse me, Mr. Abrahams, I have a question as well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: The question is that we -- the report has its probative value and that is when it establishes, prima facie or otherwise, that it has been prepared with a clinical disinterestedness, A; B, that it's not been a reflex action in preparing reports on the basis of documents; and the third is that whatever has been brought on in a tangible shape was again verified by somebody independent within the organisation to be a truthful report. For these three things, I would request you to please dilate because these things will bother us. I'm grateful.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. One of the aspects of our work that I am most proud of, personally and professionally, was our sincere attempt to document violations by all sides in this conflict. So we published reports that criticised the Serbian and Yugoslav governments, the Kosovo Liberation Army, as well as the NATO Alliance. Two in-depth reports were critical of IHL violations during the NATO bombing. In addition, the reports after the Kosovo war looked in depth at violations against Serbs by ethnic Albanians. So we bent over backwards to report in an objective and complete manner. As for the specifics in each report, our organisation's greatest asset is our credibility, which is something that takes years to build but can be destroyed in one day. So we have a rigorous internal vetting process that requires every public document to be reviewed and re-reviewed. And there were certainly times when the evidence we collected did not meet the test and we withheld publication because we did not feel comfortable putting that into the public domain. And lastly, when -- we try to be as clear about the limitations of our data so that when something a reported or alleged, we insert those qualifying terms. And when we have interviewed X number of victims whose testimony was consistent, we present that material, to allow the readers to make their own conclusion -- come to their own conclusions. So we try and present what we know and withhold what we don't so that the material is of the most use. Does that reply to your question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: I'm thankful. The next question would be that when these reports were published, are there even critiques in your notice against these reports which may also have been published or sent to you in -- through proper transmission?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The list of complaints is very long and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I mean the reports, on your reports. I'm not talking of the facts.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I understand. We never received an official criticism from either the Serbian or Yugoslav authorities or the Kosovo Liberation Army in the form of an official communication, but our reports were repeatedly criticised by -- by an -- in editorials and commentators and analysts inside Yugoslavia and abroad. And -- but to my knowledge, to my knowledge, no one to this day has found a fact to be in error. To my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: So could you tell us what was that criticism generally which may have been formulated against your reports by the press?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Most of the criticisms came from the Serbian-language press, although not exclusively, which accused us of being an anti-Serbian organisation or biased in some way against the Serbian people or nation. Again, in my public speeches and in interactions, I welcome concrete criticisms of our report in the interest of making them more accurate, but no one was able to present specific facts with evidence to make me believe we had written in error. Their complaints were of -- that we were of a political or ideological nature. My response to them was to look at our reports because we have issued a long list that criticises every side in the conflict, as well as every government in the Balkan region. And I personally have written three human rights reports critical of the Albanian government. So the arguments for bias for me are best refuted by the reports that we have published.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Just to follow up on that, did you make reports in respect to the conduct of NATO?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: Yes, we --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And was it a report of approbation or disapprobation?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: We published two reports directly in relation to the NATO bombing. One criticised the Alliance's use of cluster munitions, cluster bombs, which we considered to be indiscriminate in nature. And the second was an in-depth survey conducted in Yugoslavia, Kosovo as well as -- all of Yugoslavia, a survey of the NATO bombing, which analysed the impact of the bombing on the citizens of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: When you say "citizens" you mean civilians or --

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: I mean civilians, thank you, yes. And I can elaborate on our findings in more depth if questioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Was it approving or did you criticise them?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: No, it was a highly critical report. We determined that there were roughly 90 incidents in which NATO bombs had killed civilians, resulting in approximately 500 civilian deaths, about one-third of which were inside Kosovo. And we considered this to be a violation of international humanitarian law.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The -- back to the report As Seen, As Told. How generally -- I know this is discussed in your statement, but please tell us how generally was the information that formed the basis of the report culled?

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Sepenuk, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much, counsel, I'm guided.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Sorry, I was referring to Under Orders.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: To answer your question requires a little prelude, and I'll be brief. Under Orders is a -- has some distinct sections. One section deals with the background and the history of Kosovo, and this relied mostly on research we conducted prior to the armed conflict. The second section focuses on abuses in 19 -- from late February 1998, when we believe the armed conflict began, until the NATO bombing, March 1999. A third section deals with specifically the bombing period, NATO bombing period, to March to June 1999. And the last section deals with post-war violations after June 12th, 1999. So each of those sections has a particular -- not methodology. The methodology was the same, but to explain how the research was conducted depends on the section you are referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Let's start with the first one, the background and the history of Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: Well, this section largely -- was largely a summary of the reports we had published up and to that point. As I mentioned, our first document on Kosovo was published in 1990. A second one -- well, I'm not sure -- I believe -- I don't want to state exactly how many reports were published in that -- over the next eight years. I'm not certain of the number, but one of them was the report I researched in 1996 about police violence. So the background section was based on the research missions that we had conducted during that eight-year period.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And you participated yourself in some of those research missions?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Incidentally, although this is in your statement, do you speak Albanian?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS
utterances.text: I do speak Albanian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Stamp, would you find a suitable point at which to interrupt, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, this is a convenient moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Well, that gives me time to deal with a couple of matters. Mr. Abrahams, we have to interrupt now. That's the end of the day for us. We'll be resuming at 9.00 tomorrow morning, so we require you back here in time to start again at 9.00. You've been here before and you know the drill that you're expected and obliged not to communicate with anyone overnight in relation to your evidence, either what you've given or what you're likely to give. With that reminder, you can now leave the court and we'll see you tomorrow at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. [The witness stands down].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The matters I can deal with separately are the two issue -- two minor -- well, preliminary issues that were raised in relation to the expert witnesses Kristan and Coo. The Chamber does not regard the involvement of Kristan in the events about which his report talks as a barrier to his giving evidence. However, there are more substantial issues to be debated about whether it's appropriate for him to give evidence as an expert or whether it would be more appropriate for him to give evidence of fact on which the Trial Chamber -- or by which the Trial Chamber would be guided towards proper conclusions. But as I indicated, the broader issue is one to be addressed as we get nearer the stage of hearing his evidence. As far as Coo is concerned, the Trial Chamber consider that in this case he is too close to the team; in other words, to the Prosecution presenting the case, to be regarded as an expert. That doesn't in any way question his integrity or his effort to be independent. This is a question of perception. Justice has to not only be done but seen to be done in cases of this nature. And in this particular instance he -- the clear impression is of someone far closer to the case than would be appropriate for an expert who can express opinions on which the Chamber might rely. On the other hand, we are entirely satisfied that it's appropriate for him as an investigator to give evidence on matters of fact, and indeed we will be greatly assisted, we have little doubt, by his evidence in relation to matters of fact, identifying what documents he found. And we'll strike, I hope, the right balance in eliminating from our consideration matters of -- which we consider to be matters of opinion and concentrating exclusively on the matters of fact. Indeed, much of what he would be able to tell us as matters of fact at first sight look as though they might be opinions, but they're not. It's going to be a difficult line to draw, but I think we'll all be greatly assisted by the way the material is drawn together as long as its authenticity and reliability are established. Now, again, there will be a final opportunity to discuss his evidence before he gives it, if there's any further objection to be taken. But since we've decided that it's not appropriate he should be an expert, it may be that that resolves the matter and it's simply a question of hearing his evidence, and if there are objections to be taken as we go along on one -- on some ground or other, then these objections can be taken at that stage. Now, I hope that's a clear indication to the parties of how we view the preliminary issues that we undertook to address in relation to these witnesses. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In respect to witness Coo, can I just take it, and I think you will probably tell me that this is quite obvious from what you say, that the decision is that his report will not be received as an expert report for the reasons given.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. But we would expect you to make use of the report as a means of presenting his evidence, and it would be presented under Rule 89(F) as written material which he would be able to speak -- to vouch from the witness box.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So in other words, it would be similar to the evidence in a broad sense to the evidence that we're hearing just now. And plainly, his report refers to facts that undoubtedly will be part of the evidence in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I hear you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah. Now, I hope I've also made it clear that there is a great deal in the report which at first blush looks like opinion but really isn't. It's simply a comparison of documents and a pointer to what these appear to say, and that would be useful. But at the end of the day it will be for the Trial Chamber having that guidance to make determination about what facts to accept and what to reject and then what conclusions to draw.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Would Your Honour consider hearing further submissions from the Prosecution in this regard at a later date?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, it would be very difficult to do that, Mr. Stamp, in light of the basis for the decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: And the opportunity is not lost to you. I mean, we are still considering, and I think it is a very good decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Anyway, the -- that resolves the matter as far as he is concerned, but leaves -- for example, it -- I don't think it disturbs the first part of his report at all, and it doesn't do much to the bulk of his second report. It does, however, rule out evidence of opinion about whether there is an armed conflict or not, which we can see in the Limaj report. So that's a matter, plainly, for the Trial Chamber to determine, whether there was an armed conflict. The facts are what you ought to present for us to draw conclusions on. I don't think it's appropriate for someone in Mr. Coo's position to be telling us that that's the conclusion he's drawing in expressing that opinion as an expert. So that's the sort of area that is excluded by this decision. It may be appropriate to a further discussion about the extent to which his opinion is ex -- or what bears to be opinion is excluded nearer the time of his giving evidence. If that's the additional argument you're talking about, then that I understand. But if you want us to change our mind on whether he's an expert or not, no, it wouldn't be appropriate to advance any further arguments.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: As it pleases Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I know you want to end, but your ruling on Kristan is a little unclear to me, whether you say he's an expert or a fact witness or which one of the two?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We have not -- well, I thought I had made it clear that that has not been decided. The only question we undertook to decide at this stage in relation to Kristan was whether the fact that he had participated in some of the events was a barrier to him being regarded as an expert, and the decision on that is that it is not a barrier. I then expressed a preliminary view that his evidence might be better viewed as simply evidence of fact. He draws together a lot of material that it's useful to have in that form for the Trial Chamber to make -- to draw its own conclusions because they are largely matters of law. But I think I made it clear that that issue, whether he is an expert or not, will be resolved shortly before he gives evidence by further debate. And I was simply trying to give guidance about how we see it at first blush. And if you're able to agree on how his evidence might be presented as a result of that indication, then that would be of great assistance to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: On Coo, however, the preliminary point rules him out as an expert, so it's more a fundamental decision, but again we're only deciding the point that we undertook to decide at this stage. So we're now adjourned until 9.00 tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 14th day of July, 2006, at 9.00 a.m.
